archetype.name: Fringe Contender (pass-heavy, leaky pass protection)
archetype.definition: A .500 team with below-average efficiency, an offense that throws more than its protection can support and a middle-of-the-pack defense, good enough to stay in the AFC North race but not yet playing like a playoff team.

report.headline: A 2-2 that's honest: the run game works, the pass protection doesn't.
report.take:
Pittsburgh at 2-2 is about what its play deserves. The point differential is -2.5 per game, net EPA ranks 21st, and wins over expected sit at essentially zero. That last number stands out against history. From 2020 through 2025 this franchise beat its point differential every year, often by 1.5 to 2 wins, on top-five one-score records and turnover margins. This year the record is not ahead of the play. The 2-1 mark in one-score games is fine, but nothing about this start is being propped up by luck.

The main tension is in the play-calling. The run game is one of the league's better ones, sixth in rush EPA and 4.58 yards per carry, and they have converted every short-yardage chance. Yet Pittsburgh's pass rate over expected ranks third, behind a line that allows pressure 24% of the time (31st) and has given up 13 sacks (30th). Rodgers' time to throw is league-average at 2.87 seconds, so this isn't a quarterback holding the ball. The protection is losing. The passing game ranks 27th in EPA as a result, and the offense ranks 24th overall.

The four-game average hides a split. Weeks 1-2 were ugly: 23 points total, and a -21.8 passing EPA at New England that is the worst single performance on the sheet. Weeks 3-4 produced 54 points and positive passing EPA both times, against Cincinnati and Cleveland defenses that rank 10th and 16th. The offense may be finding its footing. The defense has moved the other way, from 13 and 20 allowed to 27 in back-to-back weeks. It gets off the field on third down (8th) and smothers short passes (8th in short EPA), but it misses tackles (29th) and gives up explosive throws (30th). Losing CB Jamel Dean and DT Derrick Harmon doesn't help.

Where it heads depends on whether the late-September offense is real. The schedule has soft spots: three 0-4 teams, and New Orleans' 30th-ranked defense. It also has Baltimore twice, Jacksonville and the rest of a division where everyone is .500 or better. This looks like a nine-win-range team whose ceiling rises if McCarthy leans into the run and the line stops leaking.

strengths.title: Efficient, physical run game
strengths.body: Pittsburgh ranks sixth in rush EPA with a top-ten stuff rate and a perfect short-yardage conversion rate. Yards before contact rank only 21st, though, so Warren and the backs are doing much of the work after contact rather than the line opening wide lanes. It should hold up, and it is underused given how often this team throws.

strengths.title: Defense wins third down and the short game
strengths.body: Opponents convert just 34.8% on third down (8th), and short passes against this defense are losing plays (8th in short EPA). With a 7.7% sack rate, that makes the underneath game hard to sustain. This is the sticky part of the defense. It forces offenses to hit big plays to score.

strengths.title: Steady takeaway production
strengths.body: The defense has two takeaways in every game box score and ranks sixth in takeaways on the season. Pittsburgh has led the league or sat near the top in turnover margin for years, so this looks like an established trait rather than noise. The offense giving the ball back has kept the margin at zero.

concerns.title: Pass protection can't support the volume
concerns.body: A 24% pressure rate allowed (31st), 31 QB hits and five sacks in the Thursday loss at Cleveland make the offense's passing lean a self-inflicted wound. It's a real line flaw, not a quarterback-timing issue, since time to throw is league-average. Unless the run share rises, expect drives to keep dying on negative plays.

concerns.title: Big plays and missed tackles
concerns.body: The defense ranks 30th in explosive pass rate allowed and 27th in deep EPA, and it misses 12.6% of tackles (29th). That's why a unit that wins third down and short passes still allowed 27 points twice in a row. With Dean doubtful for a couple of weeks, the deep shots are unlikely to get easier to stop soon.

concerns.title: Run defense is only average
concerns.body: Pittsburgh ranks 20th in rush EPA allowed and 23rd in overall success rate allowed, and Harmon's move to IR thins the interior. Opponents ran for 112 or more yards in three of four games. That matters against run-first offenses like this week's.

trend.note: The offense swung from a -21.8 passing EPA and three points at New England to 30 and 24 points with positive passing EPA the next two weeks. Meanwhile the defense went from allowing 13 to 27 twice, so the arrows are pointing in opposite directions.

nextGame.headline: Colts' thin pass rush meets Pittsburgh's worst weakness, on extra rest
nextGame.body:
Indianapolis is a run-first offense whose passing game ranks 30th in EPA, while its rushing attack ranks first. That puts the burden on Pittsburgh's average run defense and poor tackling rather than its leaky secondary. On the other side, the Colts' defense allows 393 yards a game (31st) and generates pressure only 13.8% of the time (28th), which is exactly the relief Pittsburgh's protection needs. Indy also sits at -1.5 turnovers per game, against a Steelers defense that forces two a week. The Colts' 25.5 points per game on 285 yards owes a lot to second-ranked special teams, a source of value that tends to swing.

Availability tilts toward Pittsburgh. The Colts lose DE Arden Key, a 65%-snap starter, on top of Clemons on IR, so a weak pass rush gets weaker. Keenan Allen is out and Alec Pierce is on IR, which strips the receiving corps from an already struggling passing game. Pittsburgh likely plays without CB Jamel Dean, which matters less against this passing attack, and Rico Dowdle's toe is uncertain, leaving the backfield to Warren. The Steelers also come off 10 days of rest after the Thursday game.

keyMatchups.title: Steelers' protection vs. depleted Colts rush
keyMatchups.body: Pittsburgh's 31st-ranked pressure rate allowed meets a Colts defense that ranks 28th in pressure rate and is now missing Key. This is the best chance yet for Rodgers to throw from a clean pocket, and the passing game was already trending up.

keyMatchups.title: Colts' run game vs. Steelers' tackling
keyMatchups.body: Indianapolis leads the league in rush EPA and ranks fourth in run success, while Pittsburgh ranks 20th in rush EPA allowed and 29th in missed tackles. If the Colts can stay on schedule on the ground, they shorten the game and hide a 30th-ranked passing offense.

keyMatchups.title: Turnovers and special teams
keyMatchups.body: The Colts' -1.5 turnover margin per game ranks 31st, against a Steelers defense that ranks sixth in takeaways. Indy's offsetting edge is special teams at +4.34 EPA per game. That has been a big part of how the Colts outscore their yardage, and it is the least reliable edge on either side.

nextGame.watch: Whether McCarthy keeps throwing at a top-three pass rate or leans on Warren against a run defense ranked 23rd. Either should work this week, but the sack count will tell you if the line is fixable.

restOfSeason.body:
The schedule after Indianapolis gives Pittsburgh room to climb. It includes Tampa Bay, Houston and Tennessee, all 0-4, though the Bucs' fifth-ranked defense will test this offense. New Orleans' 30th-ranked defense and Philadelphia's 29th-ranked offense add more soft spots. The back end is harder: Jacksonville, Baltimore twice and both division rematches. The defense's third-down and takeaway profile should hold up. The 27-point outings are partly a product of explosive plays, which should settle somewhat once Dean returns, but the tackling problem looks real.

Don't count on the old overperformance. This franchise has beaten its point differential for six straight years, but the 2026 team is a 21st-ranked net-EPA side, and its passing offense is held back by protection. Expect a team hovering around .500 to a game or two above. Its playoff chances depend on whether the Weeks 3-4 offense is the real version.
swingFactors: Pass protection improvement or a shift toward the run
Jamel Dean's return to the secondary
Splitting the four games against Baltimore and Cleveland

bets.reason: Pittsburgh is at home on 10 days' rest, and the matchups line up in its favor. The Colts' 28th-ranked pressure rate loses Key against the Steelers' main weakness, and Indy's -1.5 turnover margin meets a top-six takeaway defense. The Colts' 75% cover rate is propped up by second-ranked special teams, which tends to be the least repeatable edge.

Indianapolis allows 393 yards per game (31st) and 26 points per game. Pittsburgh's offense scored 30 and 24 in its last two games, and it should face the lightest pass rush it has seen. Combined with a likely short field or two from Colts turnovers, the Steelers clearing their implied number is the more likely side.

confidence.note: Four-game sample with a clear offensive split, though the injury picture is unusually clear for this matchup.
